questions.q: True or False? Imran says: 'In India, citizens are equal under the Constitution only when they speak the same language and follow the same religion.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that in India all citizens are equal under the Constitution despite differences of language, religion or culture, so equality does not depend on sameness.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: equal despite differences of language, religion or culture

questions.q: Meera was born in India, holds Indian citizenship and has worked in Singapore for fifteen years. Using the chapter's distinction between residing and being a citizen, which statement is correct?
questions.a: She is still a citizen of India, since a citizen can even reside in another country too
o: She is still a citizen of India, since a citizen can even reside in another country too
She has stopped being a citizen, because a citizen must live in the country to belong to it
She has become a citizen of Singapore, because living in a place is what makes a person a citizen
She is only a resident of India now, because her rights depend on the years she lives there

questions.q: Pooja says: 'Citizenship gives a person rights such as voting and free speech, and these rights are unlimited, because they are what make a person a citizen.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that, in a democracy, citizenship gives rights such as voting and free speech. She is wrong that they are unlimited: the chapter says these rights have limits, and that citizens also have duties like obeying the law, paying taxes, respecting others and helping keep society safe.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts that voting and free speech are rights citizenship gives
Corrects 'unlimited': rights have limits and go with duties

questions.q:
Match each situation (1-4) with the chapter's concept (A-D) it best shows.
1. Ramps are built so that a wheelchair user can enter the exhibition hall.
2. Classmates whisper that a girl 'was not of their status' and start ignoring her.
3. Families of a colony sweep the streets and clear the clogged drains on a Sunday.
4. A teacher explains that a citizen whose right is denied may approach the courts.
A. Duties   B. Rights   C. Inclusion   D. Discrimination
A neighbour says: 'Our colony's Sunday clean-up is voluntary, so it has nothing to do with being a citizen.' Which part of the chapter's account answers him best?
questions.a: Citizenship is about active participation, such as helping others in need and protecting the environment
o: Citizenship is about active participation, such as helping others in need and protecting the environment
Citizenship is only a legal identity that formally connects a person to the country
Citizenship is shown only on the days a person votes in an election
Citizenship asks something of a person only when a law orders it

questions.q: Illustrative: The toilets of a municipal school are kept locked all day, and parents say nothing. Using the chapter's account of what citizenship grants and asks, say (a) what citizens may do about the unfair practice, and (b) one duty from the chapter's list that should guide how they do it.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says citizenship grants the power to question unfair practices and stand up for what is right, so the parents may question the school's practice. (b) Duties like obeying the law and respecting others should guide them, so they ask and protest without harming anyone.
s: Part (a): question the unfair practice and stand up for what is right
Part (b): a duty such as obeying the law or respecting others

questions.q:
Illustrative: At a town festival Ravi, a street vendor's son, was turned away from the library stall while a wealthy boy was welcomed in. Some children were kept cleaning near the fair ground instead of going to school. The children went to their teacher, who told them that the Constitution gives every citizen fundamental rights: equality, freedom of speech and expression, freedom of religion, life and dignity, and education. Two of the children then argued. Kabir said, 'Let us wait until we are grown up before we raise this.' Leela said, 'Let us speak to the organisers now.'
(a) Name the right from the teacher's list that the cleaning children were denied.
(b) Predict what the teacher would say if the organisers refused every request.
(c) Whose view does the chapter's account of citizenship support, Kabir's or Leela's? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The right to education. (b) That citizens whose rights are denied have the right to approach the courts for justice. (c) Leela's, because the chapter calls citizenship active participation that grants the power to question unfair practices and stand up for what is right, and it shows the children doing so, after which changes were made; it names no age before which citizens must wait.
s: Part (a): the right to education
Part (b): approach the courts for justice
Part (c): Leela's view, with active participation and the power to question

questions.q: Sonali and Harshada first told the bullies to stop teasing Kruti, and then invited her to join their badminton team. Of the chapter's four concepts, this second step is an act of ___.
questions.a: inclusion

questions.q: A student says: 'Free speech is a right of citizens, so I can say anything I like about anyone.' Which line from the chapter's account of citizenship answers this best?
questions.a: Rights such as free speech come with limits, and citizens also have duties such as respecting others
o: Rights such as free speech come with limits, and citizens also have duties such as respecting others
Free speech is a duty that only those who pay taxes are asked to perform
Rights come to an end once a citizen goes to live in another country
Rights belong to residents of a country and not to its citizens

questions.q: A visitor says: 'The Citizenship Act of 1955 and the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of 2019 tell us everything about being a good citizen.' Using the chapter, say what these laws are said to do, and why that cannot be everything.
questions.a: The chapter says the two Acts set the rules for gaining or losing citizenship, which concerns the legal identity side. It also says citizenship is a social responsibility and about active participation, such as helping others in need, protecting the environment and standing up for those treated unfairly, as Sonali and Harshada did. So the laws cover the legal half, not all of good citizenship.
s: The Acts set the rules for gaining or losing citizenship
Citizenship is also social responsibility and active participation
Concludes the laws cover only the legal half

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's four concepts.
1. The chapter says rights, duties and discrimination are specifically mentioned in the Constitution.
2. The chapter says inclusion is specifically mentioned in the Constitution as a Fundamental Duty.
3. The chapter says citizens are equal under the Constitution only if they share one language.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
(a) State the two sides of citizenship that the chapter names.
(b) Sonali and Harshada stopped the teasing and invited Kruti into their team. Which side is this conduct an example of, and why?
questions.a: (a) Citizenship is a legal identity and a social responsibility. (b) It is the social responsibility side: the two girls held no office and made no law, but they stood up for someone who needed help and made her feel she belonged, which is how the chapter says citizenship creates a sense of belonging.
s: Part (a): legal identity and social responsibility
Part (b): social responsibility, with the reason that they stood up for Kruti and made her belong

questions.q:
'Citizenship is only a legal identity. Once the law recognises you as a citizen, nothing more is asked of you.'
(a) State what this statement gets right.
(b) Using three points from the chapter, show what it leaves out.
(c) Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) It is right that citizenship is a legal identity: it formally connects people to their country as members of its political community. (b) The chapter also calls it a social responsibility, creating a sense of belonging through shared values, rights and duties; it is about active participation such as paying taxes, helping others in need and protecting the environment; and it grants the power to question unfair practices, as the children did. (c) The statement names one half and mistakes it for the whole, so it should be rejected as incomplete.
s: Part (a): legal identity formally connects people to the country
Part (b): social responsibility and belonging
Part (b): active participation with examples
Part (b): power to question unfair practices
Part (c): a clear verdict that it is incomplete

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A citizen of a country can live in another country.
Reason (R): In a democracy, citizens have a duty to pay taxes.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Meena was kept out of the debate because of a belief that girls should not speak on stage. Gaganjit could not enter the exhibition hall because it had no ramp. In terms of the chapter's four concepts, explain why Meena's case is mainly discrimination and Gaganjit's mainly a matter of inclusion.
questions.a: Meena was treated unfairly because of her identity, her gender, which is how the chapter defines discrimination. Gaganjit was left out by the way the place was arranged, and the chapter treats ensuring no one is left out and removing barriers such as ramps as inclusion.
s: Meena: unfair treatment based on identity, which is discrimination
Gaganjit: left out by a missing facility, so inclusion and removing barriers

questions.q:
Illustrative: In a colony of 40 families, 28 take part in the Sunday clean-up and 12 never do. The colony chairman announces, 'The 12 families who never come are not citizens of India.' Nothing is known about the families except that they live in the colony and keep away from the clean-up.
(a) Work out the percentage of families that never take part.
(b) Say what the chapter says a citizen is, and whether staying away from a clean-up can by itself change that.
(c) Which side of citizenship do the 12 families fall short of?
(d) Give your verdict on the chairman's announcement, and one fair thing he could say instead.
questions.a: (a) 12 / 40 = 30 per cent. (b) A citizen is someone who legally belongs to a country and is a member of its political community; this is a formal legal membership, so staying away from a clean-up does not by itself change it. (c) The social responsibility side, since citizenship is also about active participation such as protecting the environment. (d) His announcement is wrong because it confuses legal identity with conduct; he could say that the 12 families are missing the chance to take part in what citizenship asks of them.
s: Part (a): 30 per cent
Part (b): legal membership is not changed by staying away
Part (c): the social responsibility side
Part (d): the announcement is wrong, with a fairer statement

questions.q: A colony committee decides that every notice will be printed in all three languages spoken in the colony so that no resident is left out. Which of the chapter's four concepts is this closest to?
questions.a: Inclusion, which the chapter calls an affirmative way to ensure non-discrimination
o: Inclusion, which the chapter calls an affirmative way to ensure non-discrimination
Duties, which the chapter describes as responsibilities such as obeying laws, paying taxes and keeping clean
Rights, which the chapter describes as freedoms that let people live with dignity
Discrimination, which the chapter describes as unfair treatment based on identity

questions.q: Write a short situation of two or three sentences from school life in which a student shows citizenship as a social responsibility without paying taxes or obeying a law. Then name two features of the chapter's account that your situation shows.
questions.a: Sample: Ketan notices that a new boy eats alone because he speaks little Hindi. He sits with him and invites him to the cricket game. This shows standing up for or helping someone who needs it, and creating a sense of belonging, both of which the chapter ties to citizenship as a social responsibility.
s: A believable situation that is not a tax or law case
Names one feature of the chapter's account, such as helping others or standing up for what is right
Names a second feature, such as a sense of belonging or active participation

questions.q: Write a welcome note of about eight lines for new students that the school can put on its notice board. It must: (a) define a citizen in one sentence; (b) explain in one sentence how a resident differs; (c) give two rights and two duties from the chapter's lists; (d) invite students to act like Sonali and Harshada.
questions.a: Sample: A citizen is someone who legally belongs to a country and is a member of its political community, able to take part in its decision-making. Living in a place only makes you a resident; citizenship is a formal legal membership, so a citizen can even live abroad. Citizens enjoy rights such as voting and free speech, but these have limits. They also have duties such as obeying the law and paying taxes. When you see someone teased, stop it and invite them in, as Sonali and Harshada did for Kruti.
s: A correct one-sentence definition of a citizen
Resident versus citizen stated correctly
Two rights from the chapter
Two duties from the chapter
An invitation to act, with the Kruti example or equivalent

questions.q:
(a) Which of the four concepts does the chapter call 'an affirmative way to ensure non-discrimination'?
(b) In one sentence, explain why a school that merely forbids teasing has not yet done what that concept asks.
questions.a: (a) Inclusion. (b) Forbidding teasing only stops unfair treatment, whereas an affirmative way means taking positive steps, like Sonali and Harshada inviting Kruti into their team, so that no one is left out.
s: Part (a): inclusion
Part (b): it needs positive steps to include, not only a ban on unfair treatment

questions.q:
A student's notebook has three lines on 'Who is a citizen?'. Line 1: 'A citizen is anyone who lives in a country.' Line 2: 'Citizenship gives rights like voting and free speech, but no duties.' Line 3: 'In India all citizens are equal under the Constitution despite differences of language, religion or culture.'
(a) Which line agrees with the chapter?
(b) Rewrite Line 1 so that it agrees with the chapter.
(c) Rewrite Line 2 so that it agrees with the chapter, naming two duties.
(d) Her friend says Line 2 is harmless since no one checks duties. Give the chapter's one-line reason why rights and duties should be kept together.
questions.a: (a) Line 3 agrees. (b) A citizen is someone who legally belongs to a country and is a member of its political community, able to take part in its decision-making; living in a place only makes a person a resident. (c) Citizenship gives rights like voting and free speech, which have limits, and it also brings duties such as obeying the law and paying taxes. (d) The chapter says duties are the other side of enjoying rights, and that citizens are expected to respect others and help keep society safe, so leaving them out gives a false picture of citizenship.
s: Part (a): the line on equality despite differences
Part (b): legal belonging, political community, resident distinction
Part (c): duties with two named and rights having limits
Part (d): rights and duties belong together as citizenship asks both

questions.q: A school poster says: 'Fundamental Rights are whatever we most want.' Correct the poster, using what the chapter says Fundamental Rights are and what makes them different from wishes.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights are the basic rights that every Indian citizen has, listed by the Constitution in six broad categories, and they can be enforced by law. A wish cannot be taken to a court, whereas if a Fundamental Right is violated people can approach the courts for justice.
s: Defines them as the basic rights of every Indian citizen in six categories
Says they can be enforced by law, unlike a wish

questions.q: Ishita notices that the table of key articles lists Article 21, 'protection of life and personal liberty', but Fig. 5.2 has no category called 'life'. Fig. 5.2 gives Articles 19-22 to one category. Which category must Article 21 fall under?
questions.a: The right to freedom
o: The right to freedom
The right to equality
The right against exploitation
The right to constitutional remedies

questions.q:
Match each situation (1-4) with the category of fundamental rights (A-D) that Fig. 5.2 would place it under.
1. A government post is advertised so that applicants of every caste may apply on equal terms.
2. A labourer is made to work without wages and is not allowed to leave.
3. A linguistic minority in a town opens and runs a school of its own.
4. A citizen whose right was violated goes to the Supreme Court.
A. Cultural and educational rights   B. Right to equality   C. Right to constitutional remedies   D. Right against exploitation
A school club drafts four 'rights' for its notice board. The principal asks the members to strike off the one that fails the chapter's test of a right. Which one should go?
questions.a: The right to scribble on desks whenever we feel like it
o: The right to scribble on desks whenever we feel like it
The right to express our ideas freely in every class discussion
The right to learn in a safe and respectful classroom
The right to earn a living when we grow up

questions.q:
(a) State the two-part test the chapter gives for something to count as a right.
(b) A factory owner says, 'I have a right to dump waste in the river because it saves me money.' Apply the test.
questions.a: (a) A right is what we need to live with dignity, safety and respect, and actions that cause harm to ourselves or others cannot be rights; true rights support the wellbeing and dignity of all. (b) Dumping waste harms others who depend on the river, so it fails the test and is a want, not a right.
s: Part (a): needed for dignity, safety and respect, and not harmful to self or others
Part (b): the dumping harms others, so it fails

questions.q:
Read the statements about fundamental rights.
1. Fundamental Rights can be enforced by law, so people can approach the courts if they are violated.
2. Fundamental rights protect people from unfair treatment by others and also from unfair actions by the government.
3. The chapter says not everything we want can be called a right.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: The chapter's table of key articles carries these three guarantees: (i) 'Ban on human trafficking, forced labour, and child labour'; (ii) 'Abolition of untouchability'; (iii) 'Right to approach courts to protect Fundamental Rights'. For each, say which of the six categories in Fig. 5.2 it belongs to.
questions.a: (i) The right against exploitation. (ii) The right to equality, since the chapter says the right to equality ends practices like untouchability. (iii) The right to constitutional remedies.
s: Trafficking and forced labour: right against exploitation
Untouchability: right to equality
Approaching courts: right to constitutional remedies

questions.q: A contractor brings workers from far away, withholds their wages and does not let them leave. Using the table of key articles, which guarantee speaks most directly to this?
questions.a: Articles 23-24, the ban on human trafficking and forced labour
o: Articles 23-24, the ban on human trafficking and forced labour
Article 19, freedom of speech, movement and peaceful assembly
Article 21A, free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14
Articles 29-30, protection of language, script and cultural rights

questions.q: A student argues: 'Even if I harm only myself, doing it is my right, because nobody else is affected.' Explain, using the chapter, why this still fails the test of a right.
questions.a: The chapter says actions that cause harm to ourselves or to others cannot be considered rights, so harm to oneself alone is enough to fail. Rights are what we need to live with dignity, safety and respect, and a harmful act does not serve that. True rights support the wellbeing and dignity of all, which is why the chapter calls them justified claims.
s: Cites the rule that harm to ourselves, not only others, cannot be a right
Links to rights being needed for dignity, safety and respect
Concludes with rights as justified claims supporting wellbeing of all

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'I have a right to sell spoiled food, because customers will buy it.' The chapter would reply that his wish is not a right, because the chapter sums up rights as 'justified ___'.
questions.a: claims

questions.q:
Debate motion: 'Fundamental Rights can be enforced in courts, so ordinary citizens do not need to know about them.'
(a) Quote the advice the table gives about memorising and awareness.
(b) Give two reasons from the chapter why a citizen should still know her rights.
(c) Give your verdict on the motion.
questions.a: (a) The note says citizens need not memorise the articles, but as citizens of India they should be aware of them. (b) Rights protect people from unfair treatment by others and from unfair actions by the government, and a person has to recognise that a right has been denied before she can approach the courts, as the festival children did after the teacher named their rights. The table also helps us understand how the Constitution and the Judiciary protect everyone's dignity and equality. (c) The motion should be rejected: enforceability is a reason to know the rights, not to ignore them.
s: Part (a): need not memorise, but should be aware
Part (b): first reason from the chapter
Part (b): second reason from the chapter
Part (c): a clear verdict rejecting the motion
Part (c): reason linking enforceability to awareness

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The right to constitutional remedies ensures that fundamental rights are not just promises on paper.
Reason (R): The right to constitutional remedies allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court if their fundamental rights are violated.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A letter to a newspaper says: 'Everybody wants education, so education is a right; everybody wants sweets, so sweets are a right.' Using the chapter's test, say which of the two claims passes and which fails, with the reason.
questions.a: The claim about education passes: the chapter names education among the things needed to live with dignity, safety and respect and to grow and learn. The claim about sweets fails: it is a want that the chapter's test does not count as needed for dignity, so wanting something by everyone does not make it a right.
s: Education passes, as the chapter names it as a need for dignity
Sweets fail, as a want is not a right however widely held

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Fundamental rights guard a citizen only against other citizens. The government is never bound by them, since it makes the laws.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says fundamental rights protect people from unfair treatment by others and also from unfair actions by the government, so that power is not misused. It adds that a person whose right is violated can go to court, and the right to constitutional remedies lets citizens approach the Supreme Court. Kabir has the first half of the protection but wrongly rules out the second.
s: Verdict: no
States rights protect against the government as well as others
Supports it with the court route or Article 32

questions.q: A village school charges fees and turns away an eight-year-old whose family cannot pay. Using the table of key articles, which guarantee speaks most directly to this?
questions.a: Right to free and compulsory education (6-14 years)
o: Right to free and compulsory education (6-14 years)
Equality before the law for all persons
Freedom of speech, movement and peaceful assembly
Abolition of untouchability

questions.q:
Illustrative: At a village legal-aid camp, 100 villagers were asked whether they knew that a person whose fundamental right is denied may approach the courts. 70 said they did not know. In the previous year only 5 villagers from that area had taken any such matter to court, though many had faced forced work without wages or refusal of admission to a government school.
(a) Work out the percentage who did not know.
(b) Using the chapter, explain why a right that exists in the Constitution may still go unused.
(c) Which right in Fig. 5.2 is the one that lets a villager take such a matter to the Supreme Court?
(d) The camp has time for one lesson. Should it teach the list of article numbers or the idea that rights can be enforced? Judge using the chapter's own advice on the table.
questions.a: (a) 70 / 100 = 70 per cent. (b) The chapter says these rights can be enforced, but people can only approach the courts if they know a right has been denied; the table's note says citizens should be aware of them. (c) The right to constitutional remedies, which allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court if their fundamental rights are violated. (d) The idea that rights can be enforced: the chapter says the articles need not be memorised, but citizens should be aware of the guarantees.
s: Part (a): 70 per cent
Part (b): awareness is needed to use enforceable rights
Part (c): constitutional remedies, with the reason
Part (d): teach the idea, since the chapter says no need to memorise

questions.q: Write a five-point 'Rights Help Desk' guide for your school for a student who thinks her fundamental right has been violated. It must: (a) say what a right is; (b) say where she can go; (c) name the right that makes this possible; (d) give two warnings: that not every want is a right, and that a harmful act never is.
questions.a: Sample: 1. A right is what we need to live with dignity, safety and respect, and it is a justified claim. 2. Fundamental Rights can be enforced by law, so she can approach the courts for justice. 3. For a violation she can approach the Supreme Court, which is possible because of the right to constitutional remedies. 4. Warning one: not everything we want is a right. 5. Warning two: an action that harms ourselves or others, such as damaging school property, is never a right.
s: A correct statement of what a right is
States that she may approach the courts
Names the right to constitutional remedies and the Supreme Court
First warning that a want is not a right
Second warning that harmful actions are not rights

questions.q:
The teacher at the festival named five rights: equality, freedom of speech and expression, freedom of religion, life and dignity, and education. Fig. 5.2 names six categories.
(a) Name one category in Fig. 5.2 that is not the name of any right on the teacher's list.
(b) Name one right on the teacher's list that is not itself the name of a category in Fig. 5.2.
questions.a: (a) Any one of: the right against exploitation, cultural and educational rights, or the right to constitutional remedies. (b) Any one of freedom of speech and expression, life and dignity, or education; none of these is a category name in Fig. 5.2.
s: Part (a): a category the teacher did not name: exploitation, cultural and educational, or constitutional remedies
Part (b): freedom of speech and expression, life and dignity or education

questions.q:
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly: 'If I was asked to name any particular article in this Constitution as the most important - an article without which this Constitution would be a nullity - I could not refer to any other article except this one. It is the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.' He was speaking of the right to constitutional remedies.
(a) Using what the chapter says this right ensures, explain why the Constitution would be 'a nullity' without it.
(b) Name the court the chapter says this right lets citizens approach.
(c) A classmate says, 'So the other fundamental rights are useless.' Judge this using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Without it the other fundamental rights would be just promises on paper; this right ensures that they can actually be protected and enforced. (b) The Supreme Court. (c) The remark is wrong: the chapter says fundamental rights can be enforced by law, and that this right ensures they are protected. Ambedkar's praise is for the right that guards the rest, not a statement that the rest are useless.
s: Part (a): without it the rights would be promises on paper, not protected and enforced
Part (b): the Supreme Court
Part (c): the remark is wrong because the rights are enforceable through this right

questions.q: True or False? 'Among the six categories of Fundamental Rights in Fig. 5.2 there is one whose only job is to make the other rights enforceable.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The right to constitutional remedies allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court if their fundamental rights are violated, and it ensures that the rights are not just promises on paper but can actually be protected and enforced.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the right to constitutional remedies makes the rights enforceable through the Supreme Court

questions.q: A councillor wants a scheme that takes account of the gaps history has left between groups and gives each group the support it needs. The chapter's word for this principle is ___.
questions.a: equity

questions.q: A villager says: 'In our town the rich and powerful break the rules and nothing happens to them.' Which promise of the right to equality does this practice go against?
questions.a: Every person is treated equally before the law
o: Every person is treated equally before the law
Equal opportunities in jobs and education for every adult
The end of untouchability as a practice
The bar on special titles for individuals

questions.q: The government plans to honour two people with titles: a soldier for bravery in battle and a film actor for being the most popular in the country. Using the right to equality, which of the two may it honour with a title, and why?
questions.a: It may honour the soldier. The right to equality prevents the government from giving out special titles to individuals, except for military or academic honours, and bravery in battle is a military honour whereas popularity as an actor is neither.
s: Names the soldier
Gives the rule: no special titles except military or academic honours

questions.q:
Illustrative: A school circular reads: 'Our school follows the principle of equity, so each of our 8 classes will receive the same 25 library books this year.' The school has one class whose students come from a village with no library at all, and seven classes whose families live near a public library.
(a) Which concept does the circular actually describe, going by the chapter's two panels?
(b) Explain why the circular's claim to follow equity does not hold.
(c) Rewrite one sentence of the circular so that it really follows equity.
questions.a: (a) Equality, since everyone receives the exact same support. (b) Equity means everyone gets the support they need, fairly, taking account of existing differences; the village class needs more, so identical books for all does not match need. (c) Sample: 'The class whose students have no library at all will receive extra books this year, and the other classes will receive fewer.'
s: Part (a): equality
Part (b): equity fits support to need and the village class needs more
Part (c): a sentence giving more to the class with the greater need

questions.q: A civil society organisation in a district gives free coaching to girls whose families cannot afford fees. According to the chapter, what is the organisation doing?
questions.a: Taking an initiative of the kind that aims to establish equity
o: Taking an initiative of the kind that aims to establish equity
Breaking the right to equality by treating boys differently
Doing something that only the government may do
Giving special titles to individuals for their work

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Equity means everyone gets the support they need, fairly.
Reason (R): Equity ignores existing inequalities so that all people are treated in an identical way.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Write a short notice of two or three sentences in which a college admission rule discriminates on one of the five grounds in the right to equality. Name the ground and say how the notice should be corrected.
questions.a: Sample: 'Seats in the debating club are open to boys only.' The ground is gender. It should be corrected to open the seats to every student, since the right to equality bars discrimination because of gender and ensures equal opportunities in education.
s: A notice that discriminates
Names the ground
A correction consistent with equal opportunity

questions.q: A college notice says: 'Only candidates born in our own district may apply for the hostel seats.' Using the right to equality, name the ground on which this discriminates and the guarantee it breaches.
questions.a: The ground is place of birth. It breaches the guarantee that a person cannot be discriminated against because of place of birth, and the equal opportunities in education that the right to equality ensures.
s: Names place of birth as the ground
Names the equal opportunity in education or the bar on discrimination it breaks

questions.q: A shopkeeper refuses to serve a customer because of the customer's religion. Using the table of key articles, which guarantee speaks most directly to this?
questions.a: No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth
o: No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth
End of titles (except military or academic distinctions)
Equal opportunity in public employment
Abolition of untouchability

questions.q:
A councillor says: 'Treating everyone in exactly the same way is the fairest policy, so schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao should be scrapped.'
(a) Name the concept the councillor is applying.
(b) Give the chapter's reason why the same thing for everyone may not give the same benefit.
(c) State what the campaign was meant to do.
(d) Give your verdict on his view.
questions.a: (a) Equality, in which everyone receives the exact same support. (b) Because of differences among people, which can be due to inequality and discrimination carried historically. (c) It was meant to build awareness in society and to provide support to girls' education. (d) His view should be rejected: the chapter presents such initiatives as ways to establish equity, which takes account of and addresses existing inequalities, so scrapping them in the name of identical treatment would leave the inequality in place.
s: Part (a): equality
Part (b): differences from inequality and discrimination carried historically
Part (c): awareness and support to girls' education
Part (d): a clear verdict rejecting the view
Part (d): reason using equity addressing existing inequalities

questions.q: A student says: 'Discrimination that happened long ago can have no effect on people's lives today.' Using the chapter's explanation of why the same support gives different benefits, reply to him.
questions.a: The chapter says the differences among people can be due to inequality and discrimination which may have been carried historically too. That is why the same thing given to every individual may not give the same benefit, so past discrimination can still affect people today.
s: Cites that differences may be carried historically
Links it to the same support giving different benefits

questions.q:
Read the statements about equality and equity.
1. Equity means everyone receives exactly the same support.
2. The right to equality lets the government give special titles to any individual it wishes.
3. The right to equality ends practices like untouchability.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Sana says: 'The right to equality names five grounds: religion, race, caste, gender and place of birth. So these are the only grounds on which anyone is ever discriminated against.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The five grounds are the ones named in the right to equality, but the chapter's own definition of discrimination, later on, lists more: ethnicity, disability, physical appearance, sexuality and economic background as well as caste, religion, race and gender. So the five are not the only grounds on which people are discriminated against.
s: Verdict: no
Accepts the five grounds are those the right to equality names
Names at least two further grounds from the chapter's discrimination definition

questions.q:
Illustrative: A newspaper editorial says: 'The Constitution promises equal treatment before the law to every person. Therefore every government scheme must give every citizen exactly the same thing, and schemes that give extra support to some groups are favouritism.'
(a) Which sentence of the editorial agrees with the chapter's account of the right to equality?
(b) Give the chapter's definition of equity.
(c) Does the chapter treat equity-based schemes as favouritism? Use the chapter's reasoning about the same support and different benefits.
(d) Give a verdict on the editorial: right, wrong, or partly right.
questions.a: (a) The first sentence, that every person is treated equally before the law, agrees with the chapter. (b) Equity is the quality of being fair and just, especially in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities. (c) No: the chapter says the same thing given to every individual may not give the same benefit because of differences among people, and that governments and civil society organisations take initiatives to establish equity. (d) Partly right: equal treatment before the law is right, but the conclusion that every scheme must give everyone the same thing is wrong.
s: Part (a): equal treatment before the law
Part (b): the definition of equity
Part (c): same support gives different benefits, so equity is not favouritism
Part (d): partly right, with the reason

questions.q: A club secretary is summarising the right to equality and adds four possible grounds of discrimination. Which one is NOT in the list of grounds that the chapter gives for the right to equality?
questions.a: Economic background
o: Economic background
Place of birth
Caste
Religion

questions.q:
Four situations are put to a class. For each, name the guarantee of the right to equality that is being broken. Then say which one of the four guarantees has an exception in the chapter, and what that exception is.
(i) A school bars girls from its science club.
(ii) A village head lets a landlord skip a fine that everyone else must pay for the same offence.
(iii) A family is made to sit apart at a village feast as 'untouchable'.
(iv) The government offers a special title, 'Prince of Engineers', to a rich contractor.
questions.a: (i) No discrimination on the ground of gender, and equal opportunity in education. (ii) Equal treatment before the law. (iii) The end of untouchability. (iv) The bar on the government giving special titles to individuals. The title guarantee has an exception: military or academic honours are allowed.
s: Case (i): gender and equal opportunity in education
Case (ii): equality before the law
Case (iii): the end of untouchability
Case (iv): the bar on special titles
Identifies the titles guarantee and its military or academic exception

questions.q: The chapter asks, 'Can you think of other such examples?' of equity. Give one original example from school or village life, say who it supports, and why identical help for all would not do.
questions.a: Sample: A school gives braille books to a student who is blind. It supports that student, who cannot learn from print, and the same printed book given to every student would give her no benefit.
s: A believable example of support matched to need
Says why identical help would not give the same benefit

questions.q: Illustrative: A school has 200 students and Rs 1.5 lakh to spend on travel help. Plan A gives every student Rs 500. Plan B gives every student Rs 500 and an extra Rs 1,500 to each of the 30 students who live far from school and pay more to travel. Work out the cost of each plan, say which one follows the chapter's equity idea, and give the reason.
questions.a: Plan A costs 200 x 500 = Rs 1,00,000. Plan B costs 200 x 500 + 30 x 1,500 = Rs 1,45,000, which is Rs 45,000 more but still within Rs 1.5 lakh. Plan B follows equity, because it gives the students who face a greater need the extra support, taking account of the difference among them, whereas Plan A gives everyone exactly the same.
s: Plan A cost Rs 1,00,000 and Plan B cost Rs 1,45,000
Identifies Plan B as equity
Reason: support follows need, while Plan A gives exact same to all

questions.q: A district plans a campaign with posters to change attitudes and a fund to support girls' schooling. Which chapter example is it modelled on, and under which principle does the chapter present that example?
questions.a: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, shown as an example of equity
o: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, shown as an example of equity
Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, presented as an example of strict equality
A festival-organisers' plan, presented as an example of inclusion
The abolition of titles, presented as an example of equity

questions.q:
A village committee refuses to let one group of families sit with others at a community meal, calling them 'untouchable'.
(a) Which guarantee of the right to equality does this go against?
(b) Name two of the five grounds on which the chapter says a person cannot be discriminated against.
questions.a: (a) The right to equality ends practices like untouchability. (b) Any two of religion, race, caste, gender and place of birth.
s: Part (a): the end of untouchability
Part (b): two of the five grounds

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the right to freedom comes with reasonable restrictions, it is not a real right at all.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter calls the right to freedom one of the most important rights of every Indian; the restrictions are reasonable ones that exist so that the freedoms are not misused or harmful to others or the nation, not to take the right away.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the right is important and the restrictions only prevent misuse and harm

questions.q: A town clears a street of hawkers overnight, leaving their families with no income. Which part of the right to life, as the chapter lists it, would the families point to?
questions.a: The right to livelihood, which the right to life includes
o: The right to livelihood, which the right to life includes
The right to move freely, which the right to freedom allows
The right to a special title, which the right to equality bars
The right to manage a school, which cultural rights protect

questions.q: Which of these acts could the chapter's 'reasonable restrictions' most clearly allow to be stopped?
questions.a: A student circulating a false message that damages a classmate's good name
o: A student circulating a false message that damages a classmate's good name
A student politely asking the principal to change the Sports Day dress rule
A family moving to another town in order to take up a job
A shopkeeper deciding for himself which goods he will sell

questions.q: Nisha says: 'The right to life includes a clean environment, and so courts in India have given the Ganga and Yamuna the rights of a living person for good.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: the chapter says the right to life includes a clean environment. The second half is wrong: the Uttarakhand High Court's 2017 order giving the rivers the rights of a living person was suspended and ultimately overturned by the Supreme Court as legally unsustainable, so it did not last.
s: Verdict: partly right
First half correct: clean environment is part of the right to life
Second half wrong: the order was overturned by the Supreme Court

questions.q:
Read the statements about freedom and life.
1. The right to life includes the right to health and a clean environment.
2. The right to life also protects children with disabilities, so that they can take part on an equal basis with others.
3. The right to freedom is unlimited as long as a person believes it harms nobody.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A tailor from a small town leaves it and opens a shop of his own in a big city. Which freedoms named in the chapter's right to freedom has he used?
questions.a: Moving freely and choosing how to live and work
o: Moving freely and choosing how to live and work
Practising and sharing a religion freely, since he chose a new life
Being treated equally before the law, since he is like any other person
Approaching the Supreme Court, since he left his own town

questions.q: A man is kept in custody for weeks without any hearing and without being told why. (a) Which part of the right to life, as the chapter lists it, does this concern? (b) Besides life, what else does the chapter say the right to life protects?
questions.a: (a) Fair treatment under the law. (b) Liberty: the right to life protects a person's life and liberty.
s: Part (a): fair treatment under the law
Part (b): liberty

questions.q: A court appoints people to protect and conserve a river, as the Uttarakhand High Court did in 2017 for the Ganga and Yamuna. The chapter calls such persons legal ___.
questions.a: guardians

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A citizen's right to freedom lets her do anything she likes without any limits.
Reason (R): The freedoms come with reasonable restrictions so that they are not misused or harmful to others or the nation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: A teacher says: 'Children with disabilities are not our concern; the right to life only means staying alive.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The right to life protects them, so they get the support they need to learn, play or take part on an equal basis
o: The right to life protects them, so they get the support they need to learn, play or take part on an equal basis
The right to life protects them only in hospitals and not at school
The right to education alone protects them and the right to life does not
Support for them is a favour that a school may give or withhold

questions.q:
Illustrative: A village school has 60 pupils, 4 of whom have disabilities. The classrooms are on a raised floor reachable only by steps, so these 4 cannot enter at all. The school has Rs 50,000 and can afford only one of two things: a ramp with a tactile-learning set costing Rs 40,000, or a water purifier costing Rs 35,000. A recent test showed that the school's tap water is already safe to drink.
(a) Work out how much money is left over if the school buys the ramp and learning set.
(b) Which right does the chapter say protects the 4 children, and what does it ensure for them?
(c) Which purchase fits the chapter better, and why?
(d) Name one thing the school could do next with the leftover amount, using the chapter's list of what such children should access.
questions.a: (a) 50,000 - 40,000 = Rs 10,000. (b) The right to life protects children with disabilities, ensuring they receive the support they need to learn, play or participate on an equal basis and can access education, healthcare and a safe environment. (c) The ramp and learning set, because the 4 children cannot access education at all now, while the water is already safe so the purifier would add little. (d) Sample: improve safe access to healthcare or a safe environment for those children, such as safe passage within the school.
s: Part (a): Rs 10,000
Part (b): right to life, support to learn, play or participate on an equal basis
Part (c): the ramp and learning set, since the water is already safe
Part (d): a use consistent with access to education, healthcare or a safe environment

questions.q: Write two one-sentence situations: (i) a town respects the right to a clean environment; (ii) a town fails to. Then say what the chapter says the right to life lets people do, besides merely living.
questions.a: Sample: (i) The town stops a factory's smoke from reaching the basti. (ii) The town lets a drain overflow into the children's playground for months. The chapter says the right to life means the right not only to live but to live with dignity, so that people can live safely, freely and respectfully.
s: A situation respecting a clean environment
A situation failing it
Not only to live but to live with dignity, safely, freely and respectfully

questions.q: A visitor to a school for the blind says, 'A tactile map is a luxury, not a right.' Using what the chapter says about the picture of a tactile map and about children with disabilities, reply.
questions.a: The chapter shows a tactile map as a facility that helps give effect to the right to education, and says the right to life protects children with disabilities, ensuring they get the support they need to learn on an equal basis with others. So it is part of a right, not a luxury.
s: Links the tactile map to the right to education
Cites the right to life's protection of support for children with disabilities

questions.q: A basti lies next to a factory whose smoke has made many of its children fall ill. Which part of the right to life, as the chapter lists it, is most directly affected?
questions.a: Health and a clean environment, which the right to life covers
o: Health and a clean environment, which the right to life covers
The freedom to move freely, which the right to freedom allows
The freedom to profess one's own religion without being forced
The bar on special titles, which the right to equality contains

questions.q: Show that the statement 'the right to life only means that nobody may kill you' cannot be what the chapter means, by naming three other things the chapter says the right to life includes.
questions.a: The chapter says the right to life means not only the right to live but to live with dignity, so it also includes livelihood, education, health, a clean environment and fair treatment under the law. Any three of these show that the right covers how a person lives and not only whether she is alive.
s: Quotes that it means living with dignity, not only living
Names three included items such as livelihood, health and education
Concludes that the right covers how a person lives

questions.q:
Debate motion: 'Rivers and forests cannot have legal rights; only people can.'
(a) Name two places the chapter says nature or rivers have been given legal protection and say how.
(b) State what happened to the Indian court order and why.
(c) State what the chapter's account allows you to conclude about the motion, and what it does not allow you to conclude.
(d) Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) In New Zealand the Whanganui River is legally treated as a living being; Costa Rica protects Nature's rights in its Constitution (the Uttarakhand order is a third place, later overturned). (b) The 2017 Uttarakhand High Court order making the Ganga and Yamuna legal entities with guardians was suspended and ultimately overturned by the Supreme Court as legally unsustainable. (c) It shows that some countries have given rivers or nature such rights, so 'cannot' is contradicted; it does not show that every Indian attempt must succeed, since one was overturned. (d) The motion is not supported by the chapter: legal rights for nature exist elsewhere, though the Indian order did not stand.
s: Part (a): New Zealand and Costa Rica correctly described
Part (b): overturned by the Supreme Court as legally unsustainable
Part (c): what can be concluded: such rights exist elsewhere
Part (c): what cannot be concluded: that an Indian attempt must succeed
Part (d): a clear verdict that the motion is not supported

questions.q:
(a) State what the chapter says reasonable restrictions are meant to prevent.
(b) A student posts a false rumour naming a classmate as a cheat. Explain how this shows a freedom being used in a way that is 'harmful to others'.
questions.a: (a) They are meant to prevent freedoms from being misused or being harmful to others or the nation. (b) The rumour is a use of freedom of expression that damages the named classmate, so it harms another person.
s: Part (a): not misused or harmful to others or the nation
Part (b): the rumour damages a named classmate, so it harms another person

questions.q:
(a) Name one freedom that the right to freedom allows, according to the chapter, and give an example from your own school day.
(b) Give one way the same freedom could be misused and so be restricted.
questions.a: Sample: (a) Expressing oneself: speaking in class to give an opinion on the library timings. (b) The same freedom would be misused if a student used it to spread a false rumour about a classmate, which is harmful to others, so it can be restricted.
s: Part (a): a freedom the chapter names with a real example
Part (b): a misuse that harms others and so can be restricted

questions.q:
The school council is writing a 'Freedom with Limits' charter.
(a) Give three freedoms from the chapter's right to freedom, each with a school example.
(b) Give two reasonable restrictions, each with the reason the chapter gives for such restrictions.
questions.a: Sample: (a) Express oneself: a student may give an opinion in the debate. Move freely: she may go to any library of the town. Choose how to live and work: she may choose her club activity. (b) Students may not spread false rumours, so that freedom is not harmful to others. Students may not block a meeting by shouting, so that freedom is not misused. The chapter says restrictions exist so that freedoms are not misused or harmful to others or the nation.
s: A first freedom with a school example
A second freedom with a school example
A third freedom with a school example
A first restriction with its reason
A second restriction with its reason

questions.q:
Illustrative: A plant gives 400 families their livelihood. Its smoke has made 90 of the 240 children in the neighbouring basti ill. The owner writes, 'The right to freedom lets me run my plant as I choose, and my plant gives livelihood.' The residents write, 'The right to life includes health and a clean environment.' The town must choose between two orders: Order A closes the plant for good; Order B requires the plant to fit a smoke filter costing Rs 12 lakh within six months and allows it to keep working; the plant earns about Rs 30 lakh profit a year.
(a) Work out the percentage of the basti's children who are ill.
(b) Which two parts of the right to life are in tension in this dispute?
(c) What does the chapter say about the limits of the owner's freedom?
(d) Which order fits the chapter better, and why? Use the figures.
questions.a: (a) 90 / 240 = 37.5 per cent. (b) The right to livelihood and the right to health and a clean environment. (c) Freedoms are not unlimited; they come with reasonable restrictions so that they are not misused or harmful to others or the nation. (d) Order B: the filter costs 12 / 30 = 40 per cent of one year's profit, so the plant can afford it; the chapter's restriction is aimed at the harm to others, the smoke, and the right to life also includes livelihood, so a reasonable restriction removes the harm while keeping the livelihoods.
s: Part (a): 37.5 per cent
Part (b): livelihood versus health and a clean environment
Part (c): freedom has reasonable restrictions against harm to others
Part (d): Order B, restricting the harm but keeping livelihood

questions.q: A poster in a school corridor says: 'Exploitation means any work done by a child.' Correct the poster using the chapter's definition, and say what the chapter says about child work that is acceptable.
questions.a: Exploitation means taking unfair advantage of others, often by denying them basic respect, liberty and rights, so it is not simply any work by a child. The chapter allows children below 14 to help in non-hazardous family enterprises, only during vacations or after school hours.
s: Corrected definition: taking unfair advantage by denying respect, liberty and rights
Notes the family-enterprise help allowed with its timing condition

questions.q: A broker takes twelve adult villagers to a distant town and sells them to an employer for profit. Which form of exploitation named in the chapter does this describe?
questions.a: Human trafficking
o: Human trafficking
Bonded labour
Child labour
Abuse or unfair treatment of women

questions.q: A student finds a nine-year-old working all day in a restaurant kitchen. Which course of action fits what the chapter says?
questions.a: Tell a teacher or the principal, or call the children's helpline, Childline 1098, which is available all over the country
o: Tell a teacher or the principal, or call the children's helpline, Childline 1098, which is available all over the country
Wait for the child to call the helpline herself, since it takes calls only from children
Do nothing, since the chapter allows children to work in restaurants
Look for a helpline in the town where Childline began, since it works nowhere else

questions.q: True or False? 'The right against exploitation protects only children; adults are not covered by it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the right against exploitation protects every person's dignity and safety and makes it illegal to force anyone to work against their will or under unsafe conditions. Children get special protection in addition.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: it protects every person, with extra protection for children

questions.q: Rohit says: 'The 2015 rescue shows that the helpline works only if a child calls it herself.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the call that began the 2015 rescue came from a concerned citizen, not from a child. It also says children may not understand their rights, stand up for themselves or reach help, so adults who care are often the ones who bring in the helpline.
s: Verdict: no
The call came from a concerned citizen
Links to children being unable to reach help themselves

questions.q:
Match each situation (1-4) with the form of exploitation (A-D) the chapter would name.
1. A contractor makes labourers work for months without fair wages and will not let them leave.
2. Agents move young women to another state and sell them for profit.
3. A ten-year-old is made to carry bricks all day instead of going to school.
4. A young domestic worker is repeatedly slapped and treated cruelly by her employer.
A. Human trafficking   B. Abuse or unfair treatment of women or children   C. Bonded labour   D. Child labour

Illustrative: A children's helpline logged 40 calls in one month. Of these, 25 came from concerned citizens, 10 from children themselves and 5 from other sources. A volunteer says, 'Only 10 of 40 calls came from children, so children seldom need help.'
(a) Work out the percentage of calls that came from concerned citizens.
(b) Give the reasons the chapter offers for why children may not call for help themselves.
(c) Whose call began the 2015 rescue described in the chapter?
(d) Judge the volunteer's inference using (b).
questions.a: (a) 25 / 40 = 62.5 per cent. (b) Children depend on adults for safety and wellbeing, and may not understand their rights, or be able to stand up for themselves, or access help against unfair treatment or unsafe situations. (c) A concerned citizen's. (d) The inference is not supported: a low number of children's calls does not show that children seldom need help, because the chapter says children may be unable to reach help themselves, and its 2015 case began with a call from a concerned citizen.
s: Part (a): 62.5 per cent
Part (b): depend on adults, may not know rights or reach help
Part (c): a concerned citizen
Part (d): the inference fails because children may be unable to reach help

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'Children can look after themselves, so they need no special protection.' Which reason from the chapter shows he is wrong?
questions.a: Children depend on adults for their safety and may not know their rights, stand up for themselves or reach help
o: Children depend on adults for their safety and may not know their rights, stand up for themselves or reach help
Children are weaker than adults and so tire sooner at any work
Children cannot be citizens until the age at which they can work
Children may not be protected by anyone other than their own family

questions.q: A contractor makes his labourers work for months without fair wages and will not let them leave. Among the four forms of exploitation the chapter names, this one is called ___ labour.
questions.a: bonded

questions.q: The right against exploitation makes it illegal to force anyone to work against their will or under unsafe conditions. Pick two facts from the 2015 embroidery-factory case that show these were breached, and state what action the team then took.
questions.a: The children were being forced to work, which is work against their will. They worked in a congested and unhealthy room, which is an unsafe condition. The team rescued them, provided medical care and ensured they would be taken care of, and the culprits were arrested.
s: Forced work as against their will
Congested and unhealthy room as unsafe conditions
Rescue, medical care and arrest of the culprits

questions.q: Which of these children would the chapter's rule on children below 14 allow to work?
questions.a: Priya, 13, who helps in her family's non-hazardous shop after school
o: Priya, 13, who helps in her family's non-hazardous shop after school
Maya, 12, who washes dishes in a restaurant during the school vacations
Tarun, 13, who works in a mine for a few hours on Sundays only
Sunil, 11, who helps in a factory for an hour after school hours

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Children need special protection against exploitation.
Reason (R): Children depend on adults for their safety and wellbeing and may not be able to stand up for themselves or reach help.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Write two lines for a neighbourhood poster that explain why children need special protection, using two of the chapter's reasons.
questions.a: Sample: 'Children depend on adults for their safety and wellbeing. They may not know their rights or be able to stand up for themselves, so we must stand up for them.'
s: A line using one of the chapter's reasons
A second line using a different reason

questions.q: Design a notice for a neighbourhood notice board on 'Children and Work'. It must (a) say in one line what exploitation is; (b) state the general rule for children below 14 and its exception; (c) name a place where children are banned from working; (d) say what children lose when made to work; (e) give the helpline and how to remember it.
questions.a: Sample: Exploitation is taking unfair advantage of others by denying them respect, liberty and rights. In general children below 14 may not be employed, though they may help in non-hazardous family enterprises, only during vacations or after school hours. Work in factories, mines or restaurants is banned. Children who work lose education, play and a healthy childhood. If you see a child working, call Childline 1098: count backwards from 10.
s: A correct one-line definition of exploitation
The general rule and the family-enterprise exception
A banned place such as factories, mines or restaurants
Education, play and a healthy childhood
Childline 1098 with the counting tip

questions.q:
Read the statements about exploitation and the helpline.
1. People who are forced to work without fair wages are in bonded labour.
2. Childline 1098 can be used only in the place where it first began.
3. Human trafficking means people being traded or sold for profit.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A student says Childline's number is hard to remember. (a) Using the chapter's tip, show how it can be recalled. (b) Give one reason from the chapter why children themselves may not be able to call for help.
questions.a: (a) Count backwards from 10, which gives 1098. (b) Children may not understand their rights, or be able to stand up for themselves, or access help against unfair treatment or unsafe situations.
s: Part (a): count backwards from 10
Part (b): a reason such as not knowing their rights or not being able to access help

questions.q:
Illustrative: Two 13-year-olds are said to be 'helping the family'. Asha sorts spices in her family's small, non-hazardous shop for 2 hours after school on each of 5 school days. Bilal works 6 hours a day, 6 days a week, during school hours, in a restaurant kitchen owned by a stranger. A neighbour says, 'Both should be reported, or neither.'
(a) Work out the weekly hours each child works.
(b) Say whether each case meets the chapter's conditions for children below 14 helping in work.
(c) Which, if either, is the situation the chapter describes as children made to work instead of going to school?
(d) Judge the neighbour's 'both or neither'.
questions.a: (a) Asha: 2 x 5 = 10 hours. Bilal: 6 x 6 = 36 hours. (b) Asha meets them: a non-hazardous family enterprise, outside school hours. Bilal does not: the work is in a restaurant, one of the banned places, and in school hours. (c) Bilal's. (d) The neighbour is wrong: the cases differ on the chapter's own conditions, so only Bilal's should be reported, to a teacher, the principal or a child helpline.
s: Part (a): 10 hours and 36 hours
Part (b): Asha meets the conditions and Bilal does not
Part (c): Bilal's case
Part (d): report Bilal's case only, with the reason

questions.q: Show that the statement 'children below 14 may never do any work at all' cannot be what the chapter says. Name the exception and its timing condition, and one place where the chapter bans children from working.
questions.a: The chapter says that in general children below 14 are not allowed to be employed, but they can help out in non-hazardous family enterprises, and only during vacations or after school hours. So some help is allowed. The ban is on work in places such as factories, mines or restaurants.
s: Names the non-hazardous family-enterprise exception
Gives the timing condition of vacations or after school hours
Names a banned place such as factories, mines or restaurants

questions.q:
(a) Name the three things the chapter says children lose when they are made to work.
(b) Why does it say these things matter?
questions.a: (a) Education, play and a healthy childhood. (b) The chapter says these are essential for their growth and future.
s: Part (a): education, play and a healthy childhood
Part (b): essential for growth and future

questions.q:
A village committee hears this argument: 'Poor families need the money, so children working for wages should be tolerated.'
(a) State what the chapter says children lose when they are made to work.
(b) State the general rule for children below 14.
(c) Give two steps the chapter suggests for someone who sees a child working instead of being in school.
(d) Give your verdict on the argument.
questions.a: (a) Education, play and a healthy childhood, which are essential for growth and future. (b) In general children below 14 are not allowed to be employed, though they may help in non-hazardous family enterprises, only during vacations or after school hours, and work in factories, mines or restaurants is banned. (c) Talk to a teacher or principal, or write to a child helpline. (d) The argument should be rejected: the right against exploitation protects every person's dignity and safety, and what a child loses by working is essential to her future, so need for money does not make child labour acceptable.
s: Part (a): education, play and a healthy childhood
Part (b): the below-14 rule with its exception
Part (c): two suggested steps
Part (d): a clear verdict rejecting the argument
Part (d): reason from dignity and what the child loses

questions.q: A columnist writes that Indian minority protections show 'a clash inside the Constitution'. Which statement matches how the chapter itself puts the matter?
questions.a: At times the two aims can seem to be in conflict, and some people feel that minority protections may go against secularism
o: At times the two aims can seem to be in conflict, and some people feel that minority protections may go against secularism
The courts have settled that minority protections cancel the right to equality, so the two aims never operate together
Minority protections and non-discrimination are the same thing, so the chapter sees no way in which they could seem opposed
Only minorities, and never the majority, are protected from being forced to follow a religion, so the aims never meet

questions.q: True or False? 'A government-aided school that does not promote any particular religion is not thereby stopping its students from following their own faith.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter's rule is that state-run or government-aided schools may not promote any particular religion; the right to freedom of religion still allows every person to choose, practise and share her religion freely. The rule limits what the school promotes, not what a student believes.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the rule is about the school promoting a religion, while the person's right to practise remains

questions.q: A trust orders every family in a village to pay a compulsory levy to maintain one particular temple. Which part of the right to freedom of religion does this go against?
questions.a: No one may be forced to follow, propagate or fund a religion
o: No one may be forced to follow, propagate or fund a religion
Every person may choose, practise and share her religion freely
State-run schools may not promote any particular religion
Communities may keep their own traditions and script

questions.q: Write a short speech of about eight lines for a school assembly on 'India's diversity and the right to freedom of religion'. It must say: (a) what every person may do; (b) what no one may be forced to do; (c) what state-run or government-aided schools may not do; (d) the reason the chapter gives for that school rule.
questions.a: Sample: In India people follow many religions. The right to freedom of religion lets each of us choose, practise and share our religion freely. No one may be forced to follow, propagate or fund a particular religion. State-run or government-aided schools may not promote any particular religion. The chapter says this helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state.
s: What every person may do: choose, practise and share
What no one may be forced to do: follow, propagate or fund
The school rule
The reason: protects diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state
Joins the points in order as a speech to an audience

questions.q: The chapter calls the special rights and safeguards given to groups with a different religion, language or culture ___ protections.
questions.a: minority

questions.q: Which of these is a 'minority protection' in the chapter's sense, that is, a special right or safeguard given to a group with a different religion, language or culture?
questions.a: The right of a religious or linguistic minority to set up and manage its own schools
o: The right of a religious or linguistic minority to set up and manage its own schools
A rule that every school must teach in one common language
A daily school prayer of the religion most students follow
A ban on all institutions run by minority communities

questions.q: A letter to a newspaper says: 'Letting minority communities run their own schools shows that the Constitution favours one religion.' Using the chapter's definition of minority protections and what these rights help to do, reply.
questions.a: The chapter defines minority protections as the special rights and safeguards given to groups with a different religion, language or culture, not to one religion alone, and says these rights help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality and non-discrimination.
s: Defines minority protections as safeguards for groups of different religion, language or culture
Says they help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality and non-discrimination

questions.q: Write a short situation of two or three sentences in which a government institution breaks the cultural and educational rights, then state the rule it breaks and name the four grounds the chapter lists.
questions.a: Sample: A government hostel refuses a student a seat because she belongs to a particular caste. It breaks the rule that no student can be denied admission to a government institution because of religion, caste, race or language, and those are the four grounds named.
s: A situation in which a government institution denies admission
States the rule that no student can be denied admission
Names religion, caste, race and language

questions.q: A government college refuses admission to a student only because his mother tongue is Tulu. Which protection in the chapter does this breach?
questions.a: No student may be refused admission to a government institution for her language
o: No student may be refused admission to a government institution for her language
Religious and linguistic minorities may set up and manage schools of their own
Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions as they wish
No person may be forced to follow, propagate or fund a particular religion

questions.q:
Illustrative: A government-aided school has 300 students: 270 follow Faith X and 30 follow Faith Y. Its committee considers three plans. Plan 1: keep a daily school prayer of Faith X for everyone, since most students follow it. Plan 2: forbid every student from praying anywhere on the campus. Plan 3: have no school-led prayer, while students remain free to follow and practise their own faith.
(a) Work out the percentage of students who follow Faith Y.
(b) State the rule the chapter gives for government-aided schools and the reason for it.
(c) Which plan fits both that rule and the students' right to practise their religion?
(d) Explain why the chapter's reason still rules out Plan 1 although 90 per cent of the students follow Faith X.
questions.a: (a) 30 / 300 = 10 per cent. (b) State-run or government-aided schools may not promote any particular religion, which helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state. (c) Plan 3: the school promotes no religion and every student remains free to choose and practise her own. (d) The reason is that all faiths are kept equal in the eyes of the state, so the number of followers does not entitle a school of this kind to promote one faith.
s: Part (a): 10 per cent
Part (b): the rule and its reason
Part (c): Plan 3, fitting both the rule and the right to practise
Part (d): all faiths equal in the eyes of the state, whatever the numbers

questions.q: Meghna says: 'The right to freedom of religion lets everyone choose and share her religion, so a school paid for by the government may teach one religion to all its students.' Test her claim and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The first part is right: the right allows every person to choose, practise and share her religion freely. But the chapter says state-run or government-aided schools are not allowed to promote any particular religion, which keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state, so her conclusion is wrong.
s: Verdict: no
Accepts that the right allows choosing, practising and sharing religion
Cites the rule against state-run or government-aided schools promoting a religion

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Communities in India can preserve their language, script and traditions.
Reason (R): The chapter places the right to freedom of religion in a different category of Fundamental Rights from cultural and educational rights.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A hill community runs evening classes to teach its children its own script. (a) Which category of fundamental rights in Fig. 5.2 protects this? (b) A neighbour says the classes should stop because everyone should learn only the majority language. Reply using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Cultural and educational rights. (b) The chapter says communities can preserve their language, script and traditions, so the classes are protected, and these rights help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality.
s: Part (a): cultural and educational rights
Part (b): communities can preserve their language, script and traditions

questions.q:
Read the statements about cultural and educational rights.
1. Only religious minorities, and not linguistic minorities, may set up their own schools.
2. Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions.
3. The chapter says the aim of protecting minorities and the aim of non-discrimination can never come into conflict.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Motion: 'Protections for minorities should be removed, because equality means the same rules for everyone.'
(a) State the two aims the chapter says can seem to conflict.
(b) Name two things the cultural and educational rights let minority communities do.
(c) State what the chapter says these rights help to do.
(d) Give your verdict on the motion using the chapter.
