questions.a: (a) The Constitution seeks to protect minorities and also upholds equality and non-discrimination on the basis of religion. (b) Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions, and religious and linguistic minorities can set up and manage their own schools. (c) The chapter says these rights help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality and non-discrimination. (d) The chapter does not support the motion: it presents minority protections as supporting equality and non-discrimination, and reports the conflict only as something some people feel, so it gives no ground for removing them.
s: Part (a): the two aims
Part (b): two things the rights let communities do
Part (c): help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality
Part (d): a clear verdict that the chapter does not support the motion
Part (d): reason that the conflict is only what some people feel

questions.q: A village committee tells a man he may follow his faith at home but must never speak about it to others. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: The right to freedom of religion allows every person to share her religion freely, so the order goes against it
o: The right to freedom of religion allows every person to share her religion freely, so the order goes against it
The right allows a person to follow a faith but never to share it, so the order is correct
The chapter says all religion must stay private, so the committee may order this
The order is allowed since government-aided schools may not promote religion

questions.q:
(a) What reason does the chapter give for not allowing state-run or government-aided schools to promote any particular religion?
(b) A government-aided school invites a priest of one faith to lead morning worship for all students. State what this goes against.
questions.a: (a) It helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state. (b) It goes against the rule that state-run or government-aided schools are not allowed to promote any particular religion.
s: Part (a): protects diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state
Part (b): the rule against such schools promoting a particular religion

questions.q:
Illustrative: A student's answer on religion and schools has three lines. Line 1: 'Every person may choose, practise and share her religion freely.' Line 2: 'No one can be forced to fund a particular religion.' Line 3: 'A government-aided school may promote the religion of its managers.'
(a) Which line disagrees with the chapter?
(b) Rewrite it correctly and give the chapter's reason for the rule.
(c) All three lines concern one right. Name it.
(d) Write a fourth line, true by the chapter, about cultural and educational rights.
questions.a: (a) Line 3. (b) State-run or government-aided schools are not allowed to promote any particular religion, because this helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state. (c) The right to freedom of religion. (d) Sample: Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions.
s: Part (a): Line 3
Part (b): the corrected rule with the reason
Part (c): the right to freedom of religion
Part (d): a true line on cultural and educational rights

questions.q: For each case, say which part of the chapter's account applies. (i) A girl chooses a faith that her neighbours do not follow. (ii) A village committee forces a farmer to spread a faith he does not hold. (iii) A school managed by a linguistic minority wants to run classes in its own language.
questions.a: (i) The right to freedom of religion allows every person to choose her religion freely. (ii) No one may be forced to follow, propagate or fund a particular religion. (iii) Religious and linguistic minorities have the right to set up and manage their own schools.
s: Case (i): freedom to choose a religion
Case (ii): no one forced to propagate a religion
Case (iii): minorities may set up and manage their own schools

questions.q: A girl wears her village's traditional dress on a school Culture Day, and some students laugh and tell her to wear 'modern' clothes. (a) Which protection in the cultural and educational rights supports her? (b) Which of the chapter's four concepts does the students' behaviour match, and how does the chapter define it?
questions.a: (a) Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions. (b) Discrimination, which the chapter defines as unfair treatment based on identity.
s: Part (a): communities can preserve their traditions
Part (b): discrimination, unfair treatment based on identity

questions.q: Dhruv says: 'Dharma means exactly what duty means today, and in ancient texts everyone had the same rights.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says dharma is often translated as duty but has a much wider range of meaning, including what is beneficial to people and to society, so it does not mean exactly what duty means today. It also says adhikara depended on capacity, so rights were not guaranteed universally; the one exception is that dharma implicitly gave everyone the right to justice, in theory at least.
s: Verdict: no
Dharma has a much wider range of meaning than duty
Rights depended on capacity and were not guaranteed universally

questions.q:
Match each situation (1-4) with the duty it best shows (A-D).
1. A school stands silently when the national anthem plays at the sports meet.
2. Volunteers hand out food packets in a village hit by a cyclone.
3. Students test two water samples and share their results instead of guessing.
4. Fans of a losing team refuse to damage the stadium seats.
A. Develop scientific temper   B. Abide by and respect the National Anthem   C. Protect public property and avoid violence   D. Defend the nation and help in emergencies
A student says, 'Fundamental Duties were put in the Constitution only to punish people.' Which reason does the chapter give for incorporating them?
questions.a: To remind citizens of their duties along with enjoying their fundamental rights
o: To remind citizens of their duties along with enjoying their fundamental rights
To give courts the power to punish anyone who ignores them
To take the place of the fundamental rights citizens enjoy
To list the penalties that apply for breaking each law

questions.q:
Read the statements about rights and duties.
1. Duties are enforced by law in exactly the same way as fundamental rights.
2. The duty that matches the right to express opinions freely is to listen to and respect other people's views, even when we disagree.
3. Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their duties along with enjoying their fundamental rights.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: True or False? Fundamental Duties have been a part of the Constitution since it came into effect in 1950. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that when the Constitution came into effect in 1950 it had no Fundamental Duties; they were added in 1976 by an amendment.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: no duties in 1950, added in 1976

questions.q: On an excursion, two friends are about to scratch their names on the wall of a centuries-old fort. A third student stops them, saying it is part of India's heritage. Which of the eleven duties is she acting on?
questions.a: Preserve culture and heritage
o: Preserve culture and heritage
Protect and improve the environment
Develop scientific temper
Defend the nation and help in emergencies

questions.q: Write your own right-and-duty pair from school life in the chapter's form, 'If I have the right to ..., I also have the duty to ...'. Then explain in one sentence why the chapter calls such pairs 'two sides of the same coin'.
questions.a: Sample: If I have the right to learn in a quiet classroom, I also have the duty to keep quiet when others are working. The chapter says rights and duties are not opposites but go together: rights allow us to live with dignity and duties remind us to use our freedom wisely and respectfully.
s: A right stated from school life
A matching duty stated in the chapter's form
Explains that they go together rather than oppose each other

questions.q: A teacher asks which of these is NOT among the eleven duties of Article 51A as the chapter lists them. Which one is it?
questions.a: Pay taxes every year on time
o: Pay taxes every year on time
Protect public property
Strive for excellence
Follow the freedom struggle's ideals

questions.q:
(a) A resident litters in a park. What does the chapter say about legal action for not performing a duty?
(b) A government order wrongly takes away a citizen's right. What can she do?
questions.a: (a) Duties are moral and social responsibilities that we are expected to follow, but not doing so may not always lead to legal action. (b) She can go to court for help, since rights are protected by law even against the government.
s: Part (a): moral and social responsibility, may not always lead to legal action
Part (b): she can go to court, as rights are protected by law

questions.q: A student's timeline claims that the duty about parents ensuring education for children aged 6 to 14 was among the original ten duties added in 1976. In fact it was added later, in the year ___.

Illustrative: The Class 8 council can run only one project this term. A survey of 120 students found: 42 admit dropping litter in the playground; 5 report damage to school benches; 18 did not turn up to help in the village's flood-relief drive.
(a) Work out each problem as a percentage of the 120 students.
(b) Name the Fundamental Duty to which each problem relates.
(c) Judging by how many students each problem affects, which project should the council choose?
(d) A member suggests taking offenders to court. Using the chapter, say why the council should rely on something else.
questions.a: (a) Litter: 42 / 120 = 35 per cent. Benches: 5 / 120 = about 4.2 per cent. Flood drive: 18 / 120 = 15 per cent. (b) Protect and improve the environment; protect public property and avoid violence; defend the nation and help in emergencies. (c) The litter project, because it affects the largest share, 35 per cent. (d) The chapter says duties are moral and social responsibilities, and not performing them may not always lead to legal action, so the council should rely on awareness and example.
s: Part (a): 35 per cent, about 4.2 per cent and 15 per cent
Part (b): the three duties matched correctly
Part (c): the litter project, the largest share
Part (d): duties are moral and social responsibilities with no sure legal action

questions.q: A student says, 'Rina is just an old word for a money debt.' Using the chapter, correct her and say what the chapter says naturally follows from rina.
questions.a: The chapter says rina means 'debt', but the debts we owe to devatas, ancestors and parents, gurus, fellow humans and Nature, by the very fact of being born. The duty of 'repaying' those debts naturally follows, and the chapter adds that it is more than today's sense of duty because it creates deep connections with family, society and nature.
s: Rina is a debt owed to devatas, ancestors and parents, gurus, fellow humans and Nature, not a money debt
The duty of repaying the debts follows

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rights are protected by law, while duties are moral and social responsibilities.
Reason (R): A person who does not perform a duty may not always face legal action.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rani practises her singing every day, not for a prize but to do her very best, and she helps her teammates to do the same. Which Fundamental Duty does this show?
questions.a: Strive for excellence in all activities
o: Strive for excellence in all activities
Promote harmony among all people and respect women
Preserve culture and heritage
Protect and improve the environment

questions.q:
The chapter asks: 'Imagine everyone in society enjoyed rights but ignored their duties. What would life look like?'
(a) State what the chapter says fulfilling our duties helps to do.
(b) State what the chapter says about being able to fulfil rights and duties separately.
(c) Give two things that would go wrong in a school where every student claimed rights but ignored duties, using the chapter's pairs.
(d) Give your conclusion.
questions.a: (a) Fulfilling our duties helps protect everyone's rights and keeps society fair and peaceful. (b) Rights and duties work together: you cannot fulfil one while ignoring the other. (c) Students who claim the right to be treated with respect but do not treat others with respect would lose respect for one another; students who claim the right to express opinions freely but do not listen to others' views would shout each other down. (d) Life would become unfair and unpeaceful, because rights depend on others' duties.
s: Part (a): duties protect everyone's rights and keep society fair and peaceful
Part (b): rights and duties work together
Part (c): first thing that would go wrong, using a pair
Part (c): second thing that would go wrong, using a pair
Part (d): a conclusion that rights depend on duties being done

questions.q: A father plans to stop his ten-year-old daughter from going to school so that she can work at home. Which Fundamental Duty speaks to this?
questions.a: Parents or guardians must ensure children aged 6 to 14 get an education
o: Parents or guardians must ensure children aged 6 to 14 get an education
Strive for excellence in all activities
Promote harmony among all people and respect women
Protect public property and avoid violence

questions.q: A student says, 'Fundamental Duties are optional, since nobody can be sure of being taken to court for ignoring them.' Reply using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says duties are moral and social responsibilities that we are expected to follow, even if not performing them may not always lead to legal action. Fulfilling duties also helps protect everyone's rights and keeps society fair and peaceful, so being hard to enforce in court does not make them optional.
s: Duties are responsibilities we are expected to follow, though legal action may not follow
Fulfilling duties protects everyone's rights and keeps society fair

questions.q:
Illustrative: In a Class 8 debate on whether sports clothes may be worn on Sports Day, Zoya argues strongly for her view while Arun keeps interrupting her. The teacher is considering three steps: (i) stop Zoya, because her opinions are making others uncomfortable; (ii) ask Arun to listen to and respect her view, even if he disagrees; (iii) cancel the debate.
(a) Name the right Zoya is using and the matching duty the chapter attaches to it.
(b) Say how Arun's conduct fails that duty.
(c) Which step does the chapter support, and why?
(d) Name the condition the chapter attaches to expressing views.
questions.a: (a) The right to express opinions freely; the matching duty is to listen to and respect other people's views, even when we disagree. (b) By interrupting her he refuses to listen to and respect a view he disagrees with. (c) Step (ii): the chapter pairs the right to express opinions with the duty to listen and respect, so Arun should be asked to listen. (d) That it be done without causing harm.
s: Part (a): the right and its matching duty
Part (b): interrupting fails the duty to listen and respect
Part (c): step (ii), with the reason
Part (d): without causing harm

questions.q: Using the chapter's paragraph on understanding duties, state three things the Fundamental Duties help citizens do, and give one school example for any one of them.
questions.a: The chapter says the duties help citizens play an active role in keeping democracy strong and society healthy; they help maintain good governance, promote unity, protect nature, encourage learning, and build a society where everyone can live with dignity. Sample example: students who plant saplings in the school ground protect nature.
s: Names a first thing the duties help do
Names two more things the duties help do
A correct school example for one of them

questions.q: A senior student says, 'I have the right to be treated with respect, so juniors must salute me, but I need not speak politely to them.' Which part of the chapter's pairing of rights and duties does he overlook?
questions.a: He overlooks that every right has a matching duty: if he has the right to be treated with respect, he also has the duty to treat others with respect.
s: States the principle that every right has a matching duty
Applies it: the right to respect carries the duty to treat others with respect

questions.q:
A student claims, 'Rights and duties are modern ideas. Ancient India had neither.'
(a) State what the chapter says about dharma.
(b) State what the chapter says about rina.
(c) State what the chapter says about adhikara.
(d) Judge the claim.
questions.a: (a) Dharma is often translated as duty but has a much wider range of meaning, including what is beneficial to people and society. (b) Rina is 'debt', owed to devatas, ancestors and parents, gurus, fellow humans and Nature, and it creates deep connections with family, society and nature. (c) Adhikara referred to capacity, competence or authority, the ancient word for what is now called a right, though rights then were not guaranteed universally. (d) The claim 'neither' is not supported: the chapter shows ancient ideas related to duty and to rights, although they were not the same as today's, and it says scholars have debated whether the concepts are entirely modern.
s: Part (a): dharma
Part (b): rina
Part (c): adhikara
Part (d): the claim of 'neither' is not supported
Part (d): ancient ideas differ from today's and the matter is debated

questions.q: True or False? A student who will not let a classmate sit beside her on the school bus because of the classmate's social or economic background is discriminating, even though she says nothing unkind. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says discrimination can be as subtle as not letting someone sit next to you in a school bus because of their social or economic background, and it lists economic background among the grounds.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the chapter names the bus-seat example and economic background as a ground

questions.q: Neighbours taunt a girl's family for belonging to a particular community and she stops going to school. Using the chapter's account of what discrimination does, what has happened?
questions.a: Discrimination has created a social barrier that hampers her from enjoying a fundamental right, the right to education
o: Discrimination has created a social barrier that hampers her from enjoying a fundamental right, the right to education
Discrimination has helped her enjoy her rights by making her family self-reliant
Discrimination has affected only the neighbours who spoke, not the girl or society
Discrimination has no link with rights, because it is only a matter of private opinion

questions.q: Kiran says: 'In the chapter, the drama teacher tells the class that judging someone by her looks is a form of discrimination, and Savitribai Phule's story mentions both that people believed girls should not go to school and that she was from a so-called lower caste.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes. In Sanya's story the drama teacher tells the class that excluding someone or judging them because of their looks is unfair and a form of discrimination. In Savitribai Phule's story people believed girls should not go to school, and what appalled them even more was that she was from a so-called lower caste, the Mali community. Both statements are in the chapter.
s: Verdict: yes
Sanya's story: judging by looks called a form of discrimination
Savitribai: girls' schooling opposed and lower caste both mentioned

questions.q: At auditions some students whisper that a heavily built boy 'does not fit the image' of a lead actor and urge him to take a smaller role. Which ground from the chapter's definition of discrimination does this match?
questions.a: Physical appearance
o: Physical appearance
The caste of his family
His ethnic background
His gender, as a boy

questions.q: Illustrative: A teacher always picks the same few students for every school activity, assuming the rest are 'slow'. Which words of the chapter cover this, and why would it be hard to challenge the teacher?
questions.a: The chapter lists being unwilling to include someone in a project or a celebration because of their perception of intellectual ability as indirect discrimination. It is hard to challenge because invisible discrimination is difficult to prove, and hence difficult to penalise.
s: Names the unwillingness to include someone because of perceived intellectual ability
Says invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and to penalise

questions.q:
Read the statements about discrimination.
1. Discrimination is unethical but it is not legally prohibited.
2. Discrimination affects society as a whole but not the person who is mistreated.
3. Invisible discrimination is easy to prove and therefore easy to penalise.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: None of the three
o: None of the three
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Two caselets from the chapter. Rohan's classmates make fun of his weight, nickname him 'Drummy' and make it hard for him to join their football game, and everyone around notices it. Mina does not join an overnight trip because her family cannot afford it. Some friends ignore her and whisper that she 'was not of their status'.
(a) Name the ground in each caselet.
(b) Which caselet matches the chapter's description of discrimination that may not always be visible, and which words in it show this?
(c) A student says Mina's case is not discrimination because nobody hurt or abused her. Judge his view using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Rohan: physical appearance. Mina: economic or social background. (b) Mina's: her friends ignored her and whispered about her, which is indirect, since the chapter says discrimination may be indirect, through excluding someone, and that invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and hence to penalise. (c) His view is wrong: the chapter says discrimination may be indirect, through excluding someone or being unwilling to include them because of their social background, and the ground of economic background is in its list.
s: Part (a): physical appearance and economic background
Part (b): Mina's, with ignoring and whispering as indirect exclusion
Part (c): the view is wrong because exclusion on a listed ground is discrimination without any physical harm

questions.q: A student says Savitribai Phule was abused only because she opened a school for girls. Which statement agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Two grounds combined: girls' schooling was opposed and she was from a so-called lower caste
o: Two grounds combined: girls' schooling was opposed and she was from a so-called lower caste
Only her caste mattered, since people at that time were generally supportive of girls' schooling
Only the girls' schooling mattered, and the chapter does not mention her caste anywhere at all
She was abused because her school was opened without the permission of the village

questions.q: Write a short situation of two or three sentences in which discrimination is indirect rather than open. Name the ground, and say why it would be hard to prove.
questions.a: Sample: A group of students stop talking to a boy and leave him out of the project team, whispering that he is 'not of their kind' because of his family's income. The ground is economic background. It would be hard to prove because nothing is openly said or done to him, and the chapter says invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and hence to penalise.
s: An indirect situation, not an open one
Names a ground from the chapter
Explains that invisible discrimination is hard to prove and so to penalise

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Discrimination harms only the person who is mistreated.
Reason (R): Discrimination also impacts society as a whole.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: A principal says, 'Teasing a student about her looks is only bad manners; the law is not concerned with it.' Using the chapter's definition of discrimination, reply.
questions.a: The chapter lists physical appearance among the grounds on which mistreating a person or group is discrimination, and says discrimination is not only unethical but also legally prohibited, so the law is concerned.
s: Physical appearance is a listed ground of discrimination
Discrimination is unethical and also legally prohibited

questions.q: Illustrative: In Case P, students openly mock a boy's weight in front of the whole class. In Case Q, students quietly leave a girl out of their group chat and never say why. Using the chapter, which case would be harder to prove and to penalise?
questions.a: Case Q, because indirect exclusion leaves little that can be pointed to as proof
o: Case Q, because indirect exclusion leaves little that can be pointed to as proof
Case P, because mocking in front of others cannot be shown to be discrimination
Case P, because the chapter says open mockery is never legally prohibited
Both are equally easy to prove, as the chapter treats all discrimination alike

questions.q:
A student says: 'Savitribai Phule's story is about discrimination on the ground of caste, but Anandibai Joshi's story is only about illness and has nothing to do with discrimination.'
(a) State the grounds at work in Savitribai's story.
(b) State what the chapter says Anandibai faced and did.
(c) State what the chapter says about how her life ended.
(d) Judge the student's claim.
questions.a: (a) People believed girls should not go to school, and she was from a so-called lower caste; she was abused and had mud thrown at her. (b) People were aghast at her decision to go to the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, and she was determined and fought discrimination and sustained considerable hardship. (c) She died of an illness soon after she graduated, leaving her dream unfulfilled. (d) The claim is wrong: the chapter places both stories under discrimination, and says Anandibai fought discrimination, although her death was from an illness.
s: Part (a): the girls' schooling belief and the caste ground
Part (b): people aghast, she fought discrimination and hardship
Part (c): died of illness after graduating
Part (d): a clear verdict that the claim is wrong
Part (d): reason that both stories sit under discrimination

questions.q: A teacher asks the class to find the item that is NOT a ground of discrimination in the chapter's definition of discrimination. Which one is it?
questions.a: Place of birth
o: Place of birth
Disability of any kind
Sexuality of the person
Ethnic background

questions.q:
(a) In Sanya's story, on what ground was she told she did not fit the image of a lead actor?
(b) What finally decided who got the role, and what did the students realise?
questions.a: (a) Her looks, that is her physical appearance. (b) Her expressive acting and confidence impressed the teachers, and she was chosen for an important role; the students realised that talent and effort matter far more than appearance.
s: Part (a): looks or physical appearance
Part (b): her acting and confidence, and talent and effort matter more than appearance

questions.q:
Illustrative: In Class 8 there were only 3 formal complaints of discrimination this year. In an anonymous survey, 14 of the 40 students said they had been left out of groups because of their social or economic background. The headmaster says, 'Only three complaints, so there is very little discrimination.'
(a) What percentage of the surveyed students reported being left out?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why formal complaints might be fewer than the survey shows.
(c) Name two indirect forms of discrimination the chapter lists.
(d) Judge the headmaster's conclusion.
questions.a: (a) 14 / 40 = 35 per cent. (b) The chapter says discrimination may not always be visible and that invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and hence difficult to penalise, so formal complaints would understate it. (c) Taking a jibe at somebody, excluding someone, or being unwilling to include someone in a project or a celebration. (d) His conclusion is not supported: the survey shows 35 per cent reporting exclusion, and the chapter explains why complaints would understate it.
s: Part (a): 35 per cent
Part (b): invisible discrimination hard to prove and penalise
Part (c): two forms such as a jibe, excluding, unwilling to include
Part (d): the conclusion is not supported

questions.q: A student leaves a classmate out of a group project because of the classmate's family's economic background. What does the chapter say follows for the person who discriminates in this way?
questions.a: She ethically ceases to be an active citizen of India, having breached respect and unity
o: She ethically ceases to be an active citizen of India, having breached respect and unity
She loses her Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act of 1955, as the chapter states
She loses the fundamental rights the Constitution gives to every citizen of the country
She is at once fined by the school, as the chapter requires of every student

questions.q: A teacher says, 'Discrimination is only a matter of hurt feelings.' Give three points from the chapter that show it is more than that.
questions.a: The chapter says discrimination is not only unethical but also legally prohibited. It says it affects the person or group both psychologically and physically and also society as a whole. And it creates a social barrier that hampers people from enjoying their fundamental rights.
s: Unethical and legally prohibited
Effects on the person, psychological and physical, and on society
A social barrier to enjoying fundamental rights

questions.q: Illustrative: A group never invites Latha to their birthday outings because her father sells vegetables. Is this discrimination under the chapter? Name the ground and say whether it is open or indirect.
questions.a: Yes. The ground is her social or economic background. It is indirect: the chapter lists being unwilling to include someone in a celebration because of social background as a way discrimination can be indirect.
s: Yes, with the ground of social or economic background
Indirect, as unwillingness to include someone in a celebration

questions.q: Draft a five-line 'No Discrimination' pledge for your class that: (a) defines discrimination as the chapter does; (b) names three grounds; (c) gives one subtle example from school; (d) says what discrimination does to the person; (e) commits the class to one action.
questions.a: Sample: 1. Discrimination is mistreating any person or group because of their identity or background. 2. We will not do it on grounds such as caste, religion, disability or economic background. 3. We will not leave a classmate out of a group project or a bus seat because of such a background. 4. We know it harms the person psychologically and physically, and society as a whole. 5. When we see it we will speak up and include the person.
s: Definition: mistreating a person or group because of their identity or background
Three grounds from the chapter's list
A subtle school example
The effect on the person
A commitment to act

questions.q:
Match each school situation (1-4) with the chapter's practical example of inclusion (a-d) it shows.
1. A school adds a braille section to its library.
2. Volunteers at a school fair translate between Marathi and Tamil speakers.
3. A school welcomes every child on admission day whatever her caste or religion.
4. A group waits for a classmate who reads slowly and makes sure she gets a chance to speak.
a. Finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate
b. Welcoming students from all castes, religions or backgrounds into schools
c. Giving extra help such as braille books, ramps or classroom support
d. Removing barriers to participation
A school's science club meets at 6 p.m., and few girls attend because they must be home before dark. Which step fits the chapter's idea of inclusion best?
questions.a: Move the meeting to a time when girls can attend, removing a barrier to participation
o: Move the meeting to a time when girls can attend, removing a barrier to participation
Tell the girls to arrange their own safe transport at that hour
Keep the club open to everyone on paper and wait for the girls to join
Give extra marks to the girls who manage to attend

questions.q: A panchayat holds its meeting in a hall reached by steps and only in the afternoon, when daily-wage workers cannot attend. Using the chapter's closing point on democracy, say what is wrong with this arrangement.
questions.a: The chapter says democracy is strengthened through enabling and facilitating the participation of all. The steps and the hour are barriers that keep out some people, so the meeting weakens rather than strengthens democracy.
s: States that democracy is strengthened by enabling the participation of all
Identifies the steps and the timing as barriers

questions.q: A school debating club finds that only students fluent in English join. The teacher adds sessions in Kannada and Hindi and more children begin to take part. What does this change illustrate?
questions.a: Removing a barrier to participation, so children of any fluency can join in
o: Removing a barrier to participation, so children of any fluency can join in
Giving every student the exact same support, as in the equality panel of Fig. 5.3
Offering reservations to students who are already fluent in English and Hindi
Punishing the English-speaking students for having excluded the other children

questions.q: Meera says: 'In the chapter, only a few confident readers of English joined Smt. Amita's club at first. After she added regional-language books, membership increased and all children took part, so the story shows that reservations are what make inclusion work.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is in the chapter: only a few confident readers of English joined at first, and after she added regional-language books membership increased and all children took part irrespective of their fluency. The last part is wrong: the chapter says inclusion goes beyond just giving reservations, and the club grew because of what it offered, not because of reservations.
s: Verdict: partly right
The story's facts are correctly reported
The conclusion about reservations is contradicted by the chapter

questions.q:
Read the statements about inclusion.
1. Inclusion means creating an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included.
2. Inclusion also means removing barriers to participation.
3. Inclusion is complete once reservations have been given.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Illustrative: A school of 300 students has 260 Hindi-speaking and 40 Tamil-speaking students. Its reading club runs only in Hindi, and only 6 of the Tamil-speaking students have joined. The council tried two trials. In Trial X, club notices were printed in Tamil as well; the Tamil-speaking membership rose from 6 to 8. In Trial Y, Tamil books, storytelling and puppetry were added; it rose from 6 to 18.
(a) Work out the share of the 40 Tamil-speaking students who joined in each trial.
(b) Which trial is closer to what Smt. Amita did in the chapter?
(c) Which trial should the council adopt, and why?
(d) What does the chapter say about how the children took part, whatever their fluency, after Smt. Amita's change?
questions.a: (a) Trial X: 8 / 40 = 20 per cent. Trial Y: 18 / 40 = 45 per cent. (b) Trial Y, which changed what the club offers with books and regional activities. (c) Trial Y: it raised participation far more, and it matches the chapter's idea of removing barriers to participation. (d) All children began to participate irrespective of their fluency in a particular language.
s: Part (a): 20 per cent and 45 per cent
Part (b): Trial Y
Part (c): Trial Y, by the results and by the chapter's idea
Part (d): all children took part irrespective of fluency

questions.q: Illustrative: Mohan takes longer to read and write, and in group work the others sometimes forget to wait for him. Suggest two things his group could do, and name the chapter idea they follow.
questions.a: They could be patient with him and make sure he gets a chance to speak, perhaps explaining things clearly. These follow the chapter's idea that inclusion also means removing barriers to participation, so that he is not left out.
s: Two sensible steps such as patience and giving him a chance to speak
Names removing barriers to participation, or not leaving anyone out

questions.q: Show that the claim 'a school that keeps its doors open to students of every caste, religion and background has done everything inclusion asks' cannot be right, using what the chapter says inclusion also means.
questions.a: Welcoming students from all castes, religions or backgrounds is only one of the chapter's examples. Inclusion also means giving extra help such as braille books, ramps or classroom support, finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate, making sure everyone feels accepted and supported, and removing barriers to participation. A school that only opens its doors has done the first and not the rest.
s: Says that open doors are only one example
Names at least two other things inclusion also means
Concludes that open doors alone are not enough

questions.q: A school plans extra help in the first term only for children from groups that have historically been excluded because of their social or economic background. Which statement from the chapter supports this plan?
questions.a: Inclusion is especially important for groups that have historically been excluded
o: Inclusion is especially important for groups that have historically been excluded
Inclusion applies only to children who have special needs
Equality means the same help for everyone, so the plan is wrong
Inclusion is complete once reservations have been given

questions.q: Using the chapter's two definitions, state one difference between equity and inclusion.
questions.a: Equity is the quality of being fair and just in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities, so support follows need. Inclusion is about making sure no one is left out and everyone can take part, feeling welcomed and valued with equal access to opportunities.
s: Equity as fairness that addresses existing inequalities through support
Inclusion as no one left out, with everyone welcomed and able to take part

questions.q:
Illustrative: For Sports Day a school builds a ramp at the main gate. A student who uses a wheelchair can now enter the ground, but the stands are reached by twelve steps and she watches the events from the gate. The committee announces, 'The ground is now fully inclusive.'
(a) Which part of the chapter's idea of inclusion has the ramp met?
(b) What barrier to participation remains?
(c) Judge the committee's announcement using the chapter's closing points.
questions.a: (a) Giving extra help such as ramps, one of the chapter's examples of inclusion. (b) The steps to the stands, which stop her from taking part along with the others. (c) The announcement is not justified: the chapter says inclusion means removing barriers to participation and making sure everyone feels accepted and supported, and that deliberate actions are needed to ensure it, so the remaining barrier means the job is not finished.
s: Part (a): ramps as extra help
Part (b): the steps to the stands
Part (c): barriers must be removed, so the announcement is not justified

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Inclusion goes beyond just giving reservations.
Reason (R): Inclusion means making sure everyone feels accepted and supported.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Plan an 'Inclusion Week' for your school with five activities. Each must be tied to a different idea from the chapter: (a) people speaking different languages; (b) welcoming students of all castes, religions or backgrounds; (c) extra help for children with special needs; (d) removing a barrier to participation; (e) a deliberate action that prevents discrimination.
questions.a: Sample: (a) Notices and games in the languages the students speak. (b) A welcome lunch for new students of every background. (c) A braille and large-print corner and a ramp to the hall. (d) Moving club meetings to times every student can attend. (e) A class committee that checks every event for exclusion and acts on what it finds.
s: An activity on languages
An activity welcoming students of all backgrounds
An activity of extra help for special needs
An activity that removes a barrier to participation
A deliberate action to prevent discrimination

questions.q: A college gives a seat to a student from a historically excluded community, but her classmates never speak to her. According to the chapter, has inclusion been achieved?
questions.a: Not fully, since inclusion means making sure everyone feels accepted and supported
o: Not fully, since inclusion means making sure everyone feels accepted and supported
Yes, since the chapter says that giving a place is all that inclusion requires of a college
Yes, since the chapter says classmates' behaviour is not part of inclusion at all
No, since the chapter says inclusion applies only to children with special needs

questions.q: Write a short situation of two or three sentences in which a school removes a barrier to participation for a child with special needs. Say which of the chapter's examples it matches and what the child can now do.
questions.a: Sample: A school builds a ramp to its library, and a student who uses a wheelchair can now borrow books like the others. It matches giving extra help such as braille books, ramps or classroom support to children with special needs.
s: A situation in which a barrier is removed
Matches it to the chapter's example of extra help
States what the child can now do

questions.q: The chapter says that in the Constitution fundamental rights and duties together support inclusion. Give one right and one duty from school life that together support inclusion.
questions.a: Sample: The right to education, and the duty to include a classmate who learns differently by being patient and giving her a chance to speak.
s: A right that supports inclusion
A matching duty that supports inclusion

questions.q:
A principal says: 'We give reservations in admissions, so inclusion in our school is done.'
(a) State what the chapter says about reservations and inclusion.
(b) Name two other things the chapter says inclusion means.
(c) State the closing point that bears on his words.
(d) Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says inclusion goes beyond just giving reservations. (b) It also means making sure everyone feels accepted and supported, and removing barriers to participation, for example through braille books, ramps or classroom support. (c) Deliberate actions need to be taken to prevent discrimination and ensure inclusion. (d) His claim is incomplete: reservations are not enough, and inclusion needs everyone to feel accepted and able to take part.
s: Part (a): goes beyond just giving reservations
Part (b): two other meanings of inclusion
Part (c): deliberate actions needed
Part (d): a clear verdict that his claim is incomplete
Part (d): reason that everyone must feel accepted and able to take part

questions.q: A new student who speaks only Marathi joins a class where everyone else speaks Hindi. Which of the chapter's practical examples of inclusion would help her most?
questions.a: Finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate
o: Finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate
Giving braille books to every student in the class
Building a ramp at the entrance of the school
Welcoming students into school whatever their caste

questions.q: The definition of inclusion in the chapter's list of four concepts says no one is left out because of language, religion, culture, ethnicity, caste or gender; disability is not in that list. Does building a ramp for a wheelchair user still count as inclusion in the chapter? Give the reason.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter names giving extra help like braille books, ramps or classroom support to children with special needs as an example of inclusion, and it says inclusion also means removing barriers to participation.
s: Yes, a ramp counts
Reason: ramps and support for children with special needs are examples, and inclusion removes barriers
